title: Questions and answers: relationship direction, LOAD CSV, path
text:
Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, graph projection, relationship direction
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a uniqueness constraint appears when you ask which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Elena is linked to a Group named Book circle, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Elena is linked to a Group named Book circle, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Elena'})
MERGE (b:Group {name: 'Book circle'})
MERGE (a)-[:MEMBER_OF]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Questions and answers: label, query parameter, property
text:
Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the node in graph databases
text:
A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product. Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the node as soon as they need to know which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Recommended practice: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:
Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships. It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the pattern matching as soon as they need to know which parts depend on a single factory.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Recommended practice: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Questions and answers: transaction, uniqueness constraint, community detection
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Merchant nodes and follow USED_DEVICE relationships from Account to Device.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Database nodes and follow USES relationships from Service to Database.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Transaction named TX-9005 is linked to a Merchant named TechBay, without creating duplicates
text:

```cypher
MERGE (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9005'})
MERGE (b:Merchant {name: 'TechBay'})
MERGE (a)-[:AT_MERCHANT]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the path as soon as they need to know which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Questions and answers: index, supernode, transaction
text:
Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, node, traversal
text:

A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is a traversal?

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 LIKES hops of a Person called Ben
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 LIKES hops of a Person called Ben.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})-[:LIKES*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES

```cypher
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Part nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'SHP-32' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: list every Person connected to a given Person through FRIENDS_WITH in the social network graph
text:
Task: List every Person connected to a given Person through FRIENDS_WITH in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->(b:Person)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing FRIENDS_WITH relationships, and returns the name of each Person reached. The value of $name, for example 'Grace', is passed as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: show the Author nodes whose posts is above 10 in the knowledge base graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Author nodes whose posts is above 10 in the knowledge base graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Author)
WHERE n.posts > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.posts AS posts
ORDER BY n.posts DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Author nodes above the threshold. An index on Author(posts) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow LIKES relationships from Person to Post.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 DIRECTED hops of a Person called Victor Hale
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 DIRECTED hops of a Person called Victor Hale.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Victor Hale'})-[:DIRECTED*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Article named Backup guide is linked to a Topic named Operations, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Article named Backup guide is linked to a Topic named Operations, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Article {name: 'Backup guide'})
MERGE (b:Topic {name: 'Operations'})

```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:

title: Questions and answers: transaction, pattern matching, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Cypher example: find every Account that can be reached from a Account in two steps, first through SENT and then through RECEIVED_BY

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, index, community detection
text:
Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is a index?

A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a traversal?

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a shortest path appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Questions and answers: index, uniqueness constraint, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the MERGE as soon as they need to know which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the relationship direction. Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Device nodes and follow USED_DEVICE relationships from Account to Device.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-31'})

MERGE (a)-[:SHIPS_TO]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which articles are most referenced by others, you rely directly on the PageRank.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the path. A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

In a supply chain graph with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment nodes, the idea of a transaction appears when you ask which shipments carry parts from several factories.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

In a supply chain graph with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment nodes, the idea of a uniqueness constraint appears when you ask which parts depend on a single factory.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the label as soon as they need to know how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the MERGE. MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Nora Quinn and Victor Hale are connected in the movies graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Nora Quinn and Victor Hale are connected in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Nora Quinn'})-[*..6]-(b:Person {name: 'Victor Hale'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 STORES hops of a Warehouse called Central Store
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 STORES hops of a Warehouse called Central Store.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Warehouse {name: 'Central Store'})-[:STORES*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which accounts share a device, you rely directly on the supernode.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the LOAD CSV. LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE
text:
Task: Find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: $name})-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(:Account)-[:USED_DEVICE]->(c:Device)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Device nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ACC-204' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the relationship as soon as they need to know which posts are liked by the most people.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Shipment named SHP-34 is linked to a Part named Sensor T4, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Shipment named SHP-34 is linked to a Part named Sensor T4, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-34'})
MERGE (b:Part {name: 'Sensor T4'})
MERGE (a)-[:CONTAINS_PART]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Questions and answers: PageRank, MERGE, uniqueness constraint
text:
Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Cypher example: add a new Account and connect it to a Transaction with a SENT relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Account and connect it to a Transaction with a SENT relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-205'})-[:SENT]->(b:Transaction {name: 'TX-9005'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ORD-1005 and ORD-1005 are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ORD-1005 and ORD-1005 are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Order {name: 'ORD-1005'})-[*..4]-(b:Order {name: 'ORD-1005'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

In a supply chain graph with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment nodes, the idea of a relationship direction appears when you ask which parts depend on a single factory.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

text:

A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Cypher example: add a new Article and connect it to a Article with a REFERENCES relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Article and connect it to a Article with a REFERENCES relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Article {name: 'Index tuning'})-[:REFERENCES]->(b:Article {name: 'Data modeling 101'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, traversal, aggregation
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the path as soon as they need to know which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the index as soon as they need to know what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

title: Cypher example: show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 20 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 20 in the fraud detection graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Transaction)
WHERE n.amount > 20
RETURN n.name AS name, n.amount AS amount
ORDER BY n.amount DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Transaction nodes above the threshold. An index on Transaction(amount) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: list every Service connected to a given Service through DEPENDS_ON in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: List every Service connected to a given Service through DEPENDS_ON in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(b:Service)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Service found by name, follows outgoing DEPENDS_ON relationships, and returns the name of each Service reached. The value of $name, for example 'search', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which topics an author covers, you rely directly on the uniqueness constraint.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the path. A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Article nodes and follow ABOUT relationships from Article to Topic.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Order nodes and follow REVIEWED relationships from Customer to Product.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY
text:
Task: Find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:REVIEWED]->(:Product)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(c:Category)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Category nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ORD-1004' could be passed as $name.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow OWNS relationships from Team to Service.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Article nodes and follow ABOUT relationships from Article to Topic.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-202 and ACC-205 are connected in the fraud detection graph

title: Cypher example: show the Group nodes whose members is above 50 in the social network graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Group nodes whose members is above 50 in the social network graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Group)
WHERE n.members > 50
RETURN n.name AS name, n.members AS members
ORDER BY n.members DESC

```

The WHERE clause keeps only Group nodes above the threshold. An index on Group(members) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES
text:


Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Part nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'SHP-33' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which accounts share a device, you rely directly on the shortest path.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which merchants receive money from many new accounts, you rely directly on the label.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, index, property
text:

A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, variable-length path, PageRank

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find how closely ORD-1005 and ORD-1003 are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ORD-1005 and ORD-1003 are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Order {name: 'ORD-1005'})-[*..4]-(b:Order {name: 'ORD-1003'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Transaction named TX-9003 is linked to a Account named ACC-202, without creating duplicates
text:

```cypher
MERGE (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9003'})
MERGE (b:Account {name: 'ACC-202'})
MERGE (a)-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the PageRank. PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases

title: Cypher example: make sure a Transaction named TX-9003 is linked to a Account named ACC-204, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Transaction named TX-9003 is linked to a Account named ACC-204, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9003'})
MERGE (b:Account {name: 'ACC-204'})
MERGE (a)-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Questions and answers: full-text index, supernode, relationship
text:
Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: transaction, path, selectivity
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, property, PageRank
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is good practice for the uniqueness constraint?
A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Priya
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Priya.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Priya'})-[:REVIEWED*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a supernode appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, index, query plan
text:
Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Cypher example: add a new Warehouse and connect it to a Part with a STORES relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Warehouse and connect it to a Part with a STORES relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Warehouse {name: 'East Yard'})-[:STORES]->(b:Part {name: 'Sensor T4'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Questions and answers: relationship direction, LOAD CSV, MERGE
text:

A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?

title: Cypher example: find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through DIRECTED and then through IN_GENRE
text:
Task: Find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through DIRECTED and then through IN_GENRE.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:DIRECTED]->(:Movie)-[:IN_GENRE]->(c:Genre)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Genre nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Paper Moon' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the uniqueness constraint. A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out how many movies two people have in common, you rely directly on the community detection.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: list every Merchant connected to a given Transaction through AT_MERCHANT in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: List every Merchant connected to a given Transaction through AT_MERCHANT in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: $name})-[:AT_MERCHANT]->(b:Merchant)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Transaction found by name, follows outgoing AT_MERCHANT relationships, and returns the name of each Merchant reached. The value of $name, for example 'TX-9005', is passed as a parameter.

```cypher
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Cypher example: add a new Factory and connect it to a Part with a PRODUCES relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Factory {name: 'Osaka Line'})-[:PRODUCES]->(b:Part {name: 'Valve K7'})
```

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the MERGE as soon as they need to know what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow FRIENDS_WITH relationships from Person to Person.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow RUNS_ON relationships from Service to Server.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the uniqueness constraint as soon as they need to know who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the relationship direction. Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Cypher example: find how closely TX-9005 and TX-9001 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely TX-9005 and TX-9001 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9005'})-[*..6]-(b:Transaction {name: 'TX-9001'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, query plan, node
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Service named auth-api is linked to a Database named orders-db, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Service named auth-api is linked to a Database named orders-db, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Service {name: 'auth-api'})
MERGE (b:Database {name: 'orders-db'})
MERGE (a)-[:USES]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Questions and answers: graph projection, shortest path, pattern matching
text:
Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: add a new Customer and connect it to a Product with a REVIEWED relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Customer and connect it to a Product with a REVIEWED relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Customer {name: 'Priya'})-[:REVIEWED]->(b:Product {name: 'Yoga mat'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a property appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the index.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which services are affected if a server fails, you rely directly on the traversal.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow LIKES relationships from Person to Post.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a PageRank appears when you ask which categories drive the most repeat orders.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Carla
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Carla.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Carla'})-[:MEMBER_OF*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:
A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking. It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a full-text index appears when you ask which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

text:
Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Questions and answers: index, pattern matching, label
text:
Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the LOAD CSV as soon as they need to know which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.
